- 80-100: Excellent arts, culture, or storytelling journalism. Most genuine cultural journalism belongs HERE, not below.

Doerkson led the BC Conservatives to a resounding victory on Oct. 24, and is on track to become the province's next premier, and the first from the Interior since 1986. British Columbians who didn’t stay up for the provincial election results on Saturday, Oct. 24, woke up on Sunday morning to find that the province has a new premier-in-waiting: Lorne Doerkson of the BC Conservatives, whose party swept into power for the first time since 1933. Few (if any) people still living will remember that last provincial Conservative government, but many will be asking themselves who Lorne Doerkson is. First elected provincially in the Cariboo-Chilcotin riding in 2020, as a member of the BC Liberal Party, and re-elected in 2024 as a BC Conservative, Doerkson has been extremely visible and active in his huge Interior riding — which runs from just west of Kamloops to west and north of Anahim Lake in the Chilcotin — but has largely flown under the radar during his relatively short political career. Doerkson would probably be among the first to acknowledge that his route to the premiership has been anything but typical. Of the last five B.C. premiers, three were political staffers and two were lawyers, and many MLAs start their road to the provincial legislature via local politics: the MLAs-elect for the two Kamloops ridings bordering Cariboo-Chilcotin, Peter Milobar and Ward Stamer, were first the mayors of Kamloops and Barriere respectively. Doerkson’s path was considerably different, and more colourful. Born in New Westminster in 1968, he grew up in Surrey and Salmon Arm before moving to Williams Lake in 2001. items.title: [Fast Company] Town CEO Jean-Denis Greze on why most people still don’t know what to ask AI
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

AI agents are powerful, but most ordinary people don’t yet use them. Town wants to change that. Led by CEO Jean-Denis Greze, playfully referred to as Town’s mayor, the company announced a $108 million Series B on October 19, co-led by Forerunner Ventures and Menlo Ventures, at a $1 billion valuation.  

Greze cofounded the San Francisco startup with Tony Vincent in late 2024 after serving as CTO of Plaid, where he built up the engineering team from about 20 people to 350.

Town’s betting it can make AI more accessible and practical for small-business owners and mid-market firms still looking for day-to-day AI benefits. 

Fast Company spoke with Greze about why most people still treat AI like a fancy search engine, where AI assistants can be most helpful, and why he’s working harder than he ever has before. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

ChatGPT and Claude can already connect to other apps. Why do people need stand-alone AI assistants like yours?

Could Claude or ChatGPT do most of what Town does? I think the answer is, most of it, yeah, they can. But most people who use ChatGPT or Claude aren’t using those tools to do what people in tech describe as agentic work, which just means using them to actually do things for you as opposed to researching things for you. They use it more as a Google Search replacement.

I think the biggest reason is that most people don’t really know what to put in the chat box. Putting someone in front of an empty box and asking them to write what to do, especially when the capabilities are changing all the time—that’s not onboarding.

No one’s figured out how you take a mainstream person and get them to use these products to their full potential. That’s the market opportunity. And we may be wrong, by the way. Maybe distribution just wins, and Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI end up winning. As a startup, that’s the risk you’re taking on.

What’s a use case that surprised you?

There’s a small travel firm at a vacation destination where people rent cars and gear, like a bike, for the day. The business is totally run over email. If something’s damaged, the employee takes pictures and sends an email to the central processing person.

Now there’s a little workflow that at the end of the day takes all the emails with the pictures, looks at the CRM for who the people are, and drafts the emails. They were drafting 10 to 12 of these emails every day, and it wasted 25 minutes; now it takes them 5 minutes. No one’s building SaaS for that small business. 

What should we call this category of tool? An AI assistant? A chief of staff?

We call our product a Townie. If you use the word assistant or the phrase chief of staff, you have a human mental model for what an assistant does. I think what this technology does today and what it’ll do in five years will probably defy these expectations. And no one knows what a chief of staff does outside of CEOs of Fortune 500 companies.

I actually think the right analogy for what we’re building is more like a browser or a device. When the App Store came out, suddenly a percentage of what you used to do in your web browser, you started to just do in your phone. Adding AI assistance is the same. 

The percentage of the time you interact with information in a browser or your phone will just go down now forever, and the percentage that you do by talking to an AI will go up. The future, I think, is voice for sure.

What’s next for Town?

I’m very excited about live voice. You could imagine in the morning you’re commuting to work and you have in your ear a world-class executive assistant that’s telling you, “Hey, you got seven emails overnight. There’s two of them that are urgent. On this one, if you tell me this, I can help draft the reply. The other one is going to require you to move a meeting later today. Do you want me to come up with some options?” It’s just talking to you, and you can interrupt it.

I’m also excited about what we call agent to agent. You could say, “Who at the company is really close with someone doing R&D at this other company?” Your agent will talk to other agents at your own company, and it’ll learn that Bob plays tennis with someone there. But it won’t tell you that. It’ll just be like, “Hey, Bob appears to be closely connected to that person. Do you want me to ask them if they can do the intro?” Leveraging the network of everyone within a company in a way that’s privacy-preserving is huge.

Should people connect their financial accounts to an AI agent?

If you’re a consumer, it is very likely that you connect everything about you, your medicals, your financials, to the agents. It’s just too beneficial. It’ll tell you that your credit card rate’s too high, that you should apply for a different one. It’s free money.

But the privacy concern is real. I don’t think you want to use an assistant where you’re not convinced it’s making decisions that are in your best interest. These products only work in a world where you think they truly have your best interest.

Can you trust those services?

If you’re paying for it, you can. If you’re not paying for a service, you’re not the customer. You’re being monetized in some other way.

We made the choice very early: We like consumer use cases, and they’re subsidized by business use cases. We charge businesses, and it’s not a cheap product; it’s not $5 a month. Our main plan is $50 a month.

What’s the hardest part of running Town?

The world’s too fast. I’ve never seen anything like it. It’s nerve-racking. Software had high gross margins because there was a really high fixed cost to copying it, and there was a real advantage to being early in market. By the time someone could copy you, you’d have built the next feature.

With AI, competition moves so fast and good ideas are copied so quickly. Things that would take nine months to copy are copied in a month or two.

So the pressure you feel to execute and to work a lot—I’m 47, but I’ve not worked this hard [before]. Psychologically, it’s tough, because you’re either ecstatic because you shipped something before OpenAI did, or you’re in fear that there’s a tweet from Sam Altman that puts you on your back foot. So that’s super stressful.

How do you use Town outside of work?

I’ve told Town to research food blogs and newspapers that write about food in San Francisco. I have a date night with my wife every Sunday night. So every Monday night, it looks at the next month and gives me four tables that I can make a reservation at that are classics, and then finds four that are new that have been mentioned in food blogs. I like food. I just don’t have the time [to do the research myself].

items.title: [MacRumors] Apple Ordered to Open iPhone to Rival App Stores in Australia
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Australia's Federal Court today ordered Apple to allow competing app stores, direct app downloads, and alternative payment services for Australian users from March 1, 2027.


The orders follow the court's August 2025 finding that Apple misused its market power by restricting app distribution and payment options. They cover users whose Apple Account region is Australia, with Apple Developer Program members worldwide able to participate.

Apple must let users find, download, install, and update apps through competing marketplaces and websites without charging for access or obstructing their use. Developers must receive the necessary tools on substantially the same terms as for App Store distribution, and Apple cannot penalize them for using competing stores or payment services.

Developers will also be able to offer alternative payments and link to other ways to pay, including within ‌App Store‌ apps. Apple cannot require them to offer its own purchasing system alongside alternatives, report those transactions, or allow Apple to audit them. Developers can offer lower prices through competing payment services without Apple preventing them.

The ruling also limits Apple's ability to collect fees on those purchases. It cannot charge for purchases through alternative payment services or websites in apps distributed outside the ‌App Store‌. For ‌App Store‌ apps, fees are capped at the equivalent charge for payments for physical goods or services, plus any genuine, reasonable additional costs Apple incurs for digital purchases.

Apple also cannot make alternative distribution conditional on developers offering content purchased elsewhere through its own payment system.

Security checks will remain. Apps downloaded outside the ‌App Store‌ must undergo an automated security or privacy scan and be notarized by Apple or a qualified third party. However, Apple cannot impose disproportionate installation barriers or otherwise obstruct alternative distribution. Additional security requirements for competing payments must be necessary and proportionate, with developers given an explanation in advance.

Apple can remove or disable externally installed apps only in specified cases involving harmful content, genuine security risks, or legal requirements. It cannot ban third-party apps or alternative app stores from being preinstalled on iPhones, but does not have to distribute competing stores through the ‌App Store‌.

Apple told Reuters that it plans to appeal the ruling and ask the court to pause its enforcement, citing its intellectual property rights and ‌App Store‌ security.

The changes take effect at noon Melbourne time on March 1, 2027. Apple can apply between February 1 and February 15, with supporting evidence, for a court-approved extension until May 3.

items.title: [zmescience.com] Protein evidence identifies Chinese fossils as Denisovans, revealing likely facial traits
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers have identified human fossils from Xujiayao in northern China as Denisovans using ancient proteins, then compared their bones with other remains to infer the group’s likely appearance. The fossils suggest Denisovans had low, backward-sloping foreheads, heavy brow ridges and broad, relatively flat faces, with features distinct from those of Neanderthals. The team recovered a Denisovan-linked collagen variant from two fossils with no surviving DNA. The Xujiayao collection includes 20 specimens excavated decades ago. The researchers argue that some Chinese fossils previously assigned to separate human groups may instead represent variation within the Denisovan lineage. That classification remains uncertain for specimens identified only by resemblance, and researchers say additional samples would help test it.

Reconstruction limits: Bones and molecular evidence cannot establish details such as skin tone or hairstyle, so lifelike portraits necessarily include artistic interpretation (zmescience.com).

items.title: [thestar.com] Privacy watchdog seeks details as Canadian Crime Stoppers chapters pause tips
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Police in Ottawa have suspended use of the anonymous Crime Stoppers tip service, while Crime Stoppers agencies in Saskatchewan have stopped accepting tips, as Canadian chapters respond to a breach of the P3 tip-management platform. The federal privacy commissioner is seeking more information from the platform’s vendor, Navigate360. Ottawa Police said Crime Stoppers operates independently of police and is not connected to police internal systems. They advised residents to report directly to police while they review the incident. Privacy regulators say they cannot formally investigate Crime Stoppers under their current mandates: federal privacy law generally covers commercial activity, not nonprofits, while Ontario’s watchdog oversees public-sector privacy. The federal Office of the Privacy Commissioner has nevertheless contacted Navigate360 and Crime Stoppers to offer guidance and gather information before deciding what to do next. Saskatchewan agencies said they are still seeking answers through legal counsel and described the pause as temporary.

items.title: [winnipegfreepress.com] Canadian youth climate trial tests federal emissions policy and constitutional duties
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Canada’s first youth-led federal climate trial opened Oct. 26 in Vancouver, where 15 plaintiffs argue the federal Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act and the 2030 plan fail to cut emissions enough to protect their health and safety. The plaintiffs cite personal harm from heat, wildfire smoke and extreme weather. Canada has warmed about twice as fast as the global average since 1970 and could warm 5 C by century’s end under current global policies, according to federal climate assessments cited in Canadian reporting. Plaintiffs describe smoke-related illness, displacement, flooding and drought. The federal government says Canada cannot guarantee a safe climate on its own, disputes a constitutional duty to do so and argues climate change requires a global response. Witnesses are expected to testify over four to five weeks; closing arguments are scheduled for February 2027, with a decision expected later that year.

items.title: [phys.org] Extra schooling under UK reform linked to fewer dementia diagnoses
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

A study of more than 100,000 UK Biobank participants found that a 1972 British law requiring teenagers to stay in school until 16 was associated with fewer diagnoses of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias nearly 50 years later. Using the reform’s September 1, 1957, birth-date cutoff, researchers compared people subject to different school-leaving rules and reported a 0.88% reduction in dementia incidence among those affected. Researchers also found the reduction among participants with high genetic susceptibility. They cautioned that dementia was uncommon in this cohort, whose diagnoses were tracked only through age 65, making the estimate imprecise. Continued follow-up will help determine whether the difference persists as participants age.
